title: Lumbar laminectomy for canal stenosis
subtitle: Central and lateral recess decompression without fusion

indications: Neurogenic claudication or radicular leg pain from degenerative lumbar canal or lateral recess stenosis, with concordant MRI, that limits function despite non-operative treatment (NASS guideline).
Cauda equina syndrome from stenosis is an emergency and follows the cauda equina pathway.
contraindications: Back pain alone without leg symptoms; decompression treats leg symptoms.

Dynamic instability or deformity that a decompression alone will worsen: discuss the need for fusion. In stable degenerative spondylolisthesis, randomised evidence on adding fusion is conflicting (Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study and SLIP), so the choice is individual.
Vascular claudication as the main cause of walking limitation: check pulses and ankle pressures.
preparation: MRI reviewed for the levels, the central and lateral recess components, synovial cysts and the facet orientation; standing flexion and extension radiographs when instability is suspected.
Record leg power, sensation, reflexes and bladder function; walking distance; the Oswestry Disability Index as a baseline.
Anticoagulant and antiplatelet plan agreed with the prescriber.

Consent should include dural tear and CSF leak, nerve root injury, failure to relieve symptoms, epidural haematoma with compression, infection, later instability or slip needing fusion, recurrence of stenosis, and wrong level. Mention perioperative visual loss as a rare risk of prone surgery.
positioning: Prone on a frame that keeps the abdomen free, with slight lumbar flexion to open the interlaminar spaces.
Eyes free of pressure; arms forward at no more than 90 degrees.
Image intensifier positioned for lateral views before preparing the skin.
equipment: Self-retaining retractors, Cobb elevators, Kerrison rongeurs of several sizes, Leksell rongeur, high-speed drill.
Dural repair sutures, patches and sealant.
anatomy: The ligamentum flavum attaches to the undersurface of the upper lamina and the upper edge of the lower lamina; it thickens with age and is the main soft tissue cause of stenosis.
The lateral recess lies beneath the superior articular process of the lower vertebra; the traversing root is compressed here.
The pars interarticularis connects the lamina to the pedicle; it is thin at L4 and L5 and fractures if over-thinned.
Removing more than half of each facet joint, or the pars, risks iatrogenic instability.
The dura is thin and often adherent to the ligament in severe stenosis and in revisions.
criticalSafety: Image the level before incision and before removing bone.
Keep the Kerrison footplate between the ligament and the dura; free adhesions before biting.
Preserve the pars and enough facet on each side.
Decompress the lateral recesses, not just the central canal.
structuresAtRisk: Great vessels anterior to the disc if a discectomy is added
commonErrors: Central decompression only, leaving the lateral recesses tight.
Excess facet resection, or a pars fracture.
Dural tear from biting through adherent ligament.
Failure to recognise and repair a dural tear.
complications: Dural tear with CSF leak or pseudomeningocele.
Epidural haematoma with recurrent compression or cauda equina syndrome.
Iatrogenic instability or slip, needing fusion.
Persistent leg or back pain; restenosis.
postop: Neurological observations of leg power, sensation and bladder function compared with the baseline; new weakness or retention needs urgent MRI to exclude epidural haematoma.
Mobilise early, unless a dural repair calls for a period of bed rest per surgeon preference.
Mechanical and pharmacological thromboprophylaxis per NICE NG89 and local timing after spinal surgery.
Wound check and suture removal plan.
Physiotherapy and walking programme; review at follow-up with the Oswestry score.

steps.emphasis: Read the levels from the MRI aloud and match them to the consent; record leg power and bladder function.
Slight flexion for a decompression alone; the abdomen hanging free.
Confirm a true lateral of the target levels before preparing the skin.
Count from the sacrum, check for a transitional vertebra on the MRI, and re-image on the lamina before removing bone.
Expose only to the lateral edge of the facets; preserve the facet capsules.
Only if a durotomy has occurred; repair, test with Valsalva, and tell the ward team the mobilisation plan.
Bipolar on the epidural veins and haemostatic material in the lateral gutters; ask for normotension before inspecting.
Count the cottonoids as well as swabs.
Leg power, saddle sensation and bladder function in the baseline and the trigger.
Record the levels decompressed, the extent of facet removal, and any durotomy.

step.lam.lateral-recess.title: Lateral recess and foraminal decompression
step.lam.lateral-recess.why: Leg symptoms in stenosis often come from the lateral recess and the foramen, under the superior articular process. A wide central decompression with tight lateral recesses leaves the patient with the same leg pain.
how: Undercut the medial part of the superior articular process with an angled Kerrison or a burr, staying parallel to the dura.
Follow the traversing root to its pedicle and into the foramen until a probe passes freely along it.
Remove any synovial cyst arising from the facet, separating it from the dura with care.
Repeat on the other side as needed, from the same or the contralateral approach.
pitfalls: Removing the whole facet to see the root.
Pulling an adherent synovial cyst off the dura instead of dissecting it.

step.lam.stability-check.title: Checking what is left: facets, pars and stability
step.lam.stability-check.why: Iatrogenic instability is a recognised late failure of decompression. Whether enough facet and pars remain is judged now, while it can still be changed, rather than on a radiograph months later.
how: Inspect the remaining pars on each side; if it is very thin or fractured, the segment may slip.
Estimate how much of each facet has been removed and whether the capsule is intact.
If the decompression has destabilised the segment and fusion was consented, proceed to stabilise; if it was not, finish the decompression safely and plan the next step with the patient.
Record the remaining facet and pars in the note.
pitfalls: Not recording a pars fracture, so later back pain and slip are not anticipated.

step.lam.bailout.title: Bailout: uncontrolled epidural bleeding or an unrepairable dural tear
step.lam.bailout.why: Epidural bleeding obscures the dura and roots, and blind bites in a bloody field create dural tears. A large ventral or root sleeve tear may not be repairable primarily. Recognising when to stop and change approach prevents a small problem from becoming a neurological injury.
how: Stop biting bone. Ask the anaesthetist to check the abdomen is free, the blood pressure is not high and the patient is not coughing against the tube.
Pack with haemostatic material and cottonoids, wait, then work from normal dura towards the bleeding.
For a tear that cannot be closed primarily, use a patch or muscle graft with sealant, and consider a lumbar drain per senior advice.
Call a senior colleague early if bleeding or the tear is not controlled, and record what was done.
pitfalls: Biting blindly in a pool of blood.
Leaving a tear unrepaired without telling the team.
